before: An extension method is a static method callable with instance-like syntax. This stable syntax uses this on its first parameter inside a static class.
"mint".WithBang() passes "mint" into value. LabelExtensions.WithBang("mint") calls the same static method directly.

An extension method does not gain access to private members or modify the type definition. A matching real instance member takes precedence over an extension. C# 14 also offers extension blocks; this lesson uses the older supported method syntax.
Expected behavior from this example: mint!, then goal! on separate lines. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer: Add WithPrefix(this string value, string prefix). Compare instance-like and explicit static calls. This is a separate local practice task, not a requirement to mark the reading complete.
after: An extension method is a static helper that can be called with a dot after a value. Here, it adds an exclamation mark to text.
In this syntax, a static class contains the static method, and this marks its first parameter. That parameter receives the value before the dot.
The dot-style call and the direct static call use the same method. Each passes its text into value.
The program prints mint!, then goal!. Each call returns its input text followed by an exclamation mark.

An extension method does not change the original type or gain access to its private members. A matching real instance method takes priority. C# 14 also supports extension blocks, but this older method syntax still works.
